buffer.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
buffer.text: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Back to Articles Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Published November 25, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 1 Niels Rogge nielsr Follow Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here . One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs ( sm100 ), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint . Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs , and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb . The setup The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script ( bench.py ): Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning. Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs ( control → candidate → control ). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics. Log every run in PLAN.md , including regressions and dead ends. Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner. bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled. The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure: HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver ( jobs/driver.py ) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang ( lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini ) and vLLM nightly ( vllm/vllm-openai:nightly ) in parallel. CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields. Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via hf endpoints deploy using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification. The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding. Results Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate. Config (1× RTX PRO 6000) 1-user decode (tok/s) 8-user aggregate (tok/s) Prefill 4K / 32K (tok/s) TTFT SGLang, no speculation (baseline) 134–139 543–598 18.7–19.1K / 16.9–19.1K 41–114 ms vLLM, no speculation 157.0 638 20.7K / 20.7K 33 ms SGLang + DSpark (8 drafts) 166.6 — ¹ 18.0–19.5K / 18.9–19.1K 38–51 ms vLLM + DSpark (7 drafts) 190.6 716 20.7K / 20.6K 40 ms Deployed endpoint (over the internet) 194.9 673 11.7K / 19.2K ² 198 ms ² ¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip. All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB: vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \ --tool-call-parser inkling \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser inkling \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work ). Why it stops around 190 tok/s Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job ( 1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s . Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits. Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s . At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth , so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer. What didn't work Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower: vLLM Lever Result Shorter draft length (3–6) Rejected at startup; requires num_speculative_tokens = 7 (checkpoint block size − 1). draft_sample_method: "greedy" −11% at temperature 1.0 (168.6 vs ~190.4 tok/s). rejection_sample_method: "block" 190.1 vs 190.3–190.5 for controls; no effect. enable_adaptive_verification Assertion error at startup for the Inkling 2 drafter. draft_lm_head_quantization: "fp8" Only supported for DeepSeek DSpark drafters. We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup. SGLang Lever Result Shorter draft length (3–6) Rejected at startup; requires --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8 ( gamma + 1 for the bundled drafter). SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1 +4% once, failed to reproduce against fresh controls. SGLANG_OPT_USE_FUSED_DRAFT_SAMPLE=1 +2%, within run-to-run noise. SGLANG_OPT_MOE_QUANT_ONCE=1 +1%, within run-to-run noise. SGLANG_DSPARK_USE_GREEDY_DRAFT=1 −9% at temperature 1.0 (156.8 vs ~172 tok/s). Benchmarking gotchas A few measurement issues caught us along the way: Triton JIT during timed prefill. vLLM's first 4K prefill came back at 202 tok/s instead of 20K because Triton was compiling kernels during the timed request. Running an unmeasured warmup across prompt lengths and concurrency fixed 4K prefill, though the first run in each Job still under-reported 32K prefill due to last-chunk shape

buffer.title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
buffer.text: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton Back to Articles Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton Enterprise + Article Published November 24, 2026 Upvote 5 Oluwaseun Doherty seun-doherty Follow nvidia Oyindamola Omotuyi OOyindamola Follow nvidia Richard AntRi31 Follow nvidia TL;DR Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment. Introduction A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy. NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing. 1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab For simulation and training, prepare: A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements. Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager. For physical-robot testing, prepare: A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task. A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded. A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles. Quick install Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies: git lfs install git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git cd IsaacLab uv sync --frozen Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets: uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets Download the walking policy Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically. uv run isaaclab play \ --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \ --rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \ --num_envs 1 --visualizer none \ --video newton_gl --video_length 1 \ presets=backlash 2. Build the obstacle course The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box , office bin , bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready. uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \ --repo-type dataset \ --revision 9d4556bfe80868c1d27a7a7ba1c2774e63e8cedd \ --include "box_cardboard_a01/*" \ --include "trashCan_office_black_a03/*" \ --include "table_bedside_b01/*" \ --local-dir ./assets/simready At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows. Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles. Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry. 3. Understand how ToF sensing guides the walking policy The IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior. During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment. Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls. The obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle . Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py , ToF sensing is in sensors.py , and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/ . Model the ToF sensor MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck. Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately. # Selected settings; mount and raycast targets omitted. head_tof = MicroDuckToFCameraCfg( prim_path=MICRODUCK_HEAD_BODY_PATH, update_period= 1.0 / 15.0 , pattern_cfg=patterns.PinholeCameraPatternCfg( focal_length= 1.0 , width= 8 , height= 8 , horizontal_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, vertical_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, ), randomization=ToFRandomizationCfg( mount_pitch_degrees=(- 10.0 , 10.0 ), mount_height_m=(- 0.02 , 0.02 ), floor_validity_midpoint_offset_m=( 0.0 , 0.13 ), near_floor_edge_impairment_probability= 0.5 , ), data_types=[ "distance_to_image_plane" , "distance_to_camera" ], max_distance=TOF_MAX_RANGE, depth_clipping_behavior= "zero" , ) 4. Train the Microduck policy across parallel environments Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets. The 16,384 environments shown here are configurable, not a minimum requirement. Lower --num_envs to fit your GPU’s available memory. With fewer environments collecting experience in parallel, reaching comparable policy performance may require more training iterations and longer training time. We also trained this policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates, demonstrating a smaller-scale configuration for the same workflow. Run this command to train the policy: uv run isaaclab train \ --task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \ --rl_library rsl_rl \ --num_envs 16384 \ --max_iterations 1500 \ --seed 42 \ --device cuda:0 \ --visualizer none \ presets=backlash Figure 2. Parallel MicroDuck obstacle-avoidance simulation 5. Inspect behavior and export the policy to ONNX Playback uses the same props, primitives, frozen walker and sensor randomization as training, with a different seed for new obstacle arrangements. Navigation checkpoints are saved under logs/rsl_rl/microduck_obstacle_avoidance_tof_flat_backlash/<timestamp>/ relative to the repository root. Choose a model_<iteration>.pt file from your run and replace /absolute/path/to/model.pt below with its path. This plays the policy, opens the Newton viewer and records 20 seconds of simulation. Set --viz to none for headless recording. uv run --extra video isaaclab play \ --task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \ --rl_library rsl_rl \ --checkpoint /absolute/path/to/model.pt \ --num_envs 1 \ --seed 6173 \ --device cuda:0 \ --viz newton_gl \ --video newton_gl \ --video_length 1000 \ presets=backlash Playback saves TorchScript and ONNX models in the checkpoint’s exported folder. Keep the ONNX data file alongside the model. Figure 3. Cone-course evaluation with requested motion, policy steering, and ToF input overlays. 6. buffer.title: From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity
buffer.text: Identifying Molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Antigravity â Google DeepMind Skip to main content November 25, 2026 Science From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity Robert Brunck, Stefan Ganscha, Swaroop Guntupalli, Dariusz Lasecki, Gabriella Marfani, Jack Mason, Hussain Masoom, Rose Mirshafian, Eliseo Papa and Zoi Tsangalidou Explore Science on Google Antigravity Share Built in collaboration with analytical chemists and using community-developed tools, Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra, lay out chemical evidence, and match frontier-level retrieval accuracy even with a lightweight model. Every sample of blood, soil or plant tissue contains a vast array of small molecules, such as nutrients, hormones, drugs and their breakdown products, pollutants, or bioactive compounds with therapeutic potential. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of these molecular signals in a single drop of sample extract, measuring the masses of charged molecules and, in tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), the fragments they break into. These measurements, however, do not directly reveal the molecular structure. Researchers cannot immediately tell which compound produced a signal and relate it to its biological role or downstream use cases. To fully map the diversity of small molecules, which remains largely uncharted, researchers need ways to translate mass spectra to molecular structures at scale. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra from previously measured molecules. Yet even after a decade of expanding reference libraries, spectral searches annotate on average only about 5% of measured spectra, and 10% for human samples; the rest has been called the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry. Many of the molecules producing these unannotated signals are already listed in public chemical databases, but their spectra have not been recorded, so there is no reference spectrum to compare against. Elucidating them instead requires inferring the structure directly from the observed fragment ions. Analytical chemists have a well-tested, step-by-step workflow for narrowing down candidate structures from tandem (MS/MS) spectra: check spectral reference libraries, find the molecular formula and retrieve candidate structures from chemical databases, and then test every candidate against observed fragment peaks. The tools for each step exist and are openly available, but running the full workflow would take a domain expert a significant amount of time for every single spectrum. Because a single study can produce thousands of spectra, manual analysis cannot keep up, leaving most of these signals unannotated. Today, we are sharing Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity , a suite of domain skills that pair Gemini's chemical reasoning with the ability to run established mass spectrometry tools and query public chemical databases on the user's behalf to fulfil their request. Antigravity runs these skills, combines their results, and reasons about the chemistry, laying out the evidence for a chemist to review. For molecules that are already catalogued in a database, identification is much faster. For undiscovered molecules, the agent still helps: it narrows down the formula and the parts of the structure supported by the fragments to guide full structure elucidation. A language model cannot do this on its own, since matching fragments to a structure takes precise mass calculations, searches across databases of millions of compounds, and simulations of how bonds break. Pairing Geminiâs reasoning with dedicated chemistry tools brings those steps into one workflow. Antigravity and the Mass Spec Skills have the potential to transform our natural product-based drug discovery workflows by substantially accelerating the identification of bioactive compounds from complex plant extracts. Their remarkable accuracy in predicting even highly complex molecular structures (>90% in most of our evaluations), coupled with detailed interpretation of MS/MS fragmentation patterns, could significantly reduce the time required for compound annotation and enable us to prioritise promising bioactive candidates more rapidly and confidently. Dr Phanankosi Moyo University of Pretoria Figure 1. How a molecule is identified from its tandem mass spectrum: prepare the signal, search reference libraries, deduce the formula and rank candidate structures, then cross-check and refine. Each step is carried out by our Mass Spec Skills built on established, openly available tools. Researchers can describe their task and any instrument-specific tolerances in plain language without having to configure each underlying tool. The agent selects and chains the relevant skills, lowering the technical barrier to entry for scientists less familiar with computational tools. From a single prompt, the agent can take an unannotated tandem mass spectrum all the way to a proposed chemical structure and an auditable report (Figure 2). Figure 2. The agent preprocesses the raw recording, identifies the molecular formula C 20 H 21 ClN 6 O, ranks 845 PubChem isomers against simulated fragments and neutral losses, and summarises the evidence alongside the top candidate structure. It also compiles a detailed report mapping predicted fragment substructures onto 14 of the 19 signal peaks (97.7% of summed fragment intensity). Each stage of that workflow can also be run on its own for smaller everyday tasks, from cleaning up a noisy recording to annotating peaks or comparing candidate isomers: Slide 1 of 6 Spotting the precursor ion and removing baseline noise: the agent converts the negative-mode precursor peak at m/z 395.1387 ([MâH]â) into a neutral molecular mass of 396.1459 Da. Using matchms with configurable intensity thresholds, it strips out over 1,700 low-intensity background noise spikes from the raw recording, leaving a clean spectrum of fragment signals ready for structural analysis. Checking public spectral libraries for known compounds: the agent queries experimental MS/MS reference libraries ( GNPS and MoNA ) using user-specified or instrument-matched mass tolerances, scoring de-noised fragment peaks by cosine similarity. In this example, the search returns no high-confidence library match, prompting the agent to fall back to formula prediction and chemical database search. Pinning down the exact elemental composition: combining the neutral mass with SIRIUS fragmentation-tree scoring across ten candidate elements, the agent identifies the chlorinated formula C 20 H 21 ClN 6 O at â1.5 ppm mass error (score 37.86, well ahead of the runner-up at 28.33) and confirms that the main fragment formulas add up to the intact molecule. Assigning fragments and diagnostic neutral losses: using MAGMa , MetFrag , and pairwise neutral-loss lookup, the agent accounts for 97.7% of the summed fragment intensity (matching 14 of the 19 preprocessed peaks). It links the measured peaks through sequential neutral losses of hydrogen chloride (HCl) and isocyanic acid (HNCO), placing a chlorine atom and a urea group on the same half of the molecule. Breaking a score tie with reaction chemistry: when top isomers in PubChem account for the exact same share of the preprocessed spectrum (97.7% of summed fragment intensity across 14 of 19 peaks), the agent tests whether their bond connectivity and functional groups match the observed fragmentation pathways, ruling out candidates that lack a central urea linkage and identifying the top candidate that explains the major cleavages. Validating the final molecule and its cleavage sites: the agent verifies with RDKit that the winning structure is chemically valid and matches the exact mass and formula, then draws the 2D molecule and highlights the central bond cleavage that produces the dominant fragment pair. Antigravity and Mass Spec Skills takes a big leap forward from what we currently can do with MS/MS data. The ability to formulate de novo structure predictions, informed by existing knowledge minable through agentic AI, reduces a complicated process - one that previously required days or months of analysis and literature review - to a matter of hours. For natural products, this instantly creates a tool chemists can use to prioritize or de-prioritize features in their data towards metabolite classes of interest, enabling smarter and vastly accelerated workflows towards drug discovery. Dr Scott Jarmusch Assistant Professor at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) From raw spectrum to structure end-to-end To see how the chemical evidence fits together in practice, consider the negative-mode tandem mass spectrum from the end-to-end run in Figure 2 (precursor [MâH]â at m/z 395.1387; Figure 3). buffer.title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
buffer.text: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA Back to Articles An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 5 Vrunda Gadesha vrunda-gadesha Follow ibm-research Cyril Shaji cyrilshaji Follow ibm-research Jobit Treesa Varughese jotreesa1 Follow ibm-research Nivetha Suruliraj nivetha-suruliraj Follow ibm-research Anu Sugunan anu24-hugface Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Jaydeep Sen JaydeepSen Follow ibm-research Amith Singhee asinghee Follow ibm-research Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type. We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps . The use case: a Farm Assistant A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent: Listens and turns the speech into text. Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English. Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says. Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked. If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up. Where CUGA fits CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things: One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting. The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search() . Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's. The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it. audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server. The hard part is not the voice Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval : a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph. Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning. The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large ), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything. Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages. Making it sound right and keeping it safe A few small decisions mattered more than we expected: Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech. Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC , and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast. Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user. Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key. Try it You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer: CUGA Apps on Hugging Face → Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA , starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn. Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent. Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust. This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity. buffer.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
buffer.text: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents Back to Articles Where scientists draw the line on AI agents Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 5 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work. These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings. To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies. Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used. One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust : validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research. Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized. A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge. Helping researchers check the work For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually. But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs. Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis. But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way. Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows. These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks. These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like. Keep scientific judgment in the loop Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process? An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?” Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves. Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation. Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said. Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research. These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work. The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. facts: Google DeepMind introduced Mass Spec Skills for the Google Antigravity platform.

It automates the workflow of identifying molecular structures from mass spectrometry data.
The system integrates with established tools like SIRIUS, MAGMa, MetFrag, and RDKit.
It addresses the 'dark matter' of mass spectrometry where most signals remain unannotated.

facts: IBM Research released an Indic Voice Agent built on the open-source CUGA agent harness.

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) handles agent wiring, tool management, and guardrails.
The system uses multilingual embedding models to enable cross-lingual retrieval between Indic languages and English documents.
The agent is designed to provide grounded answers from specific documents, such as agricultural handbooks.

week_log.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
facts: Inkling 2 Mini features ~26B total parameters with 3B active per token.
The model uses a looped Mixture-of-Experts architecture with 24 physical layers.
Inference optimization on an RTX PRO 6000 achieved 190.6 tok/s using vLLM and DSpark.
The model supports a 1M-token context window.
Performance was improved by 40% compared to baseline configurations.
The optimization process used a coding agent to run 46 benchmark experiments.
The model checkpoint uses mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 precision.
DSpark speculative decoding was essential for reaching 95% of the hardware memory-bandwidth ceiling.

week_log.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
facts: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) interviewed 17 scientists on the responsible development of AI agents.
Five dimensions of scientific trust were identified: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency.
Researchers expressed concerns about AI agents overlooking conflicting evidence or making unsupported claims.
There is a need for clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted scientific work.
Participants highlighted the risk of AI-assisted research diminishing human learning and intellectual contribution.
Ai2 is exploring participatory benchmarks where scientists help define safety requirements for AI agents.
Scientists emphasized that delegating tasks to AI does not remove the researcher's responsibility for the work.
Interviewees were divided between enthusiasm for AI-driven progress and existential concerns about the role of human scientists.

week_log.title: Can language models drive a humanoid robot? Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 November 25, 2026
facts: Artificial Analysis introduced AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 to evaluate frontier language models on controlling a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
The benchmark includes ten household and industrial tasks across four skill groups: embodied reasoning, pick and place, assembly/tool use, and mobility.
GPT-6.2 Astra leads the benchmark with a score of 71.0.
Models are given five practice episodes in new scenes to write code and notes before being evaluated on ten additional unseen scenes.
The simulation uses NVIDIA Isaac Sim and the Unitree G1 robot with 29 joints and three-fingered hands.
Every model achieved a perfect score on the mobility task (warehouse navigation).
Pick and place tasks were the weakest performance area for all models due to difficulties with the robot's three-fingered hands.
GPT-6.2 Sol is the fastest model at 17.3 minutes per evaluation episode, while Claude Fable 5.2 is the most expensive at $9.01 per episode.

594641133.source: Ai2 released RoboTrack, a benchmark and training suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench includes 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse. RoboTrack-15M is a new synthetic training dataset containing 15 million point tracks generated via MolmoSpaces. The suite includes two new models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. RoboTracker is a fine-tuned version of AllTracker, while RoboTracker-Warp is based on CoWTracker. Evaluations show existing trackers perform significantly worse on real-world manipulation tasks than on previous benchmarks. RoboTracker-Warp achieved state-of-the-art performance on four out of five evaluated benchmarks. The research aims to improve robot perception for complex tasks like pipette handling in wet-lab environments. RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation Back to Articles RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation Enterprise Article Published November 23, 2026 Upvote 4 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark Deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes. One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking . Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions. Robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice. We introduce RoboTrack , a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 , and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces , Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M , a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation. RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos. Our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks. Today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp . RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results. RoboTrack-Bench: A benchmark for point-tracking in real-world manipulation RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 | Artificial Analysis Artificial Analysis K All articles November 25, 2026 Can language models drive a humanoid robot? Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 gives frontier language models control of a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot across ten household and industrial tasks. Today’s research preview of our simulation benchmark follows last month’s preview of AA-Robotics v0.1, our work with physical robot arms in our lab. In AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1, each model practices five episodes per task, keeps only the notes and code it wrote, and is then scored on ten new evaluation scenes with different rooms, lighting and task details. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 Frontier language models can now write and run code well enough to act in the physical world. AA-Robotics v0.1 was our first step, with models controlling a robot arm. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 evaluates frontier language models on their ability to control a simulated humanoid robot, which has to walk, look around, and use two dexterous hands at once. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 is our research preview of the simplest experiment we have designed to test this: language models in coding agent harnesses directly controlling a humanoid. Each model is given control of a simulated Unitree G1, with 29 joints, three-fingered hands and a head camera, and a simple objective for each task. It is the next step in our work measuring AI agents in simulated robotics, and we plan to expand from here. For each task, the model is first given five practice episodes back to back, each in a new scene, to learn the environment and take notes. Only the files it writes (memory, notes, code and skills) are kept. Using these, the model is then evaluated on ten new scenes, each with a different room, lighting, layout and task details, and each in a fresh run that starts from a copy of those files. We find that some skills are already mature, while others are missing from every model. Every model walked the robot to the goal without moving a package in every navigation episode, and most played the full melody on the toy piano in most episodes. But no model reliably loaded the dishwasher, with only five dishes ending in the rack in 90 episodes, and none finished with a single item of laundry in the washing machine.
